name: JPL Horizons API
summary: High-precision ephemerides, state vectors and orbital elements for solar system bodies and spacecraft from NASA/JPL Horizons.
description: Horizons computes observer tables (RA/Dec, azimuth/elevation, magnitude, rise/set), vector tables (position and velocity) and osculating elements for planets, moons, asteroids, comets and many spacecraft, from any observing site. Requests use quoted parameters on a single GET endpoint that returns JSON wrapping a text table; a POST batch-file variant also exists.

rate_limit.summary: Not documented on the pages I fetched.

endpoints.summary: Ephemeris, vectors or elements for a target body

example.response_excerpt:
{"signature":{"source":"NASA/JPL Horizons API","version":"1.2"},"result":"...Target body name: Mars (499) ... Center body name: Earth (399) ...
$$SOE
 2026-Nov-11 00:00     ...
$$EOE
..."}

license.name: US Government work (NASA/JPL); no licence statement on the API page

agent_notes: String parameter values must be wrapped in single quotes (%27 when encoded). The table sits inside result between $$SOE and $$EOE, so parse that text. COMMAND takes a numeric id or a name, ambiguous names return a list of matches instead of an ephemeris. Centre 500@399 is geocentric Earth.
caveats: From my sandbox the TLS chain was not trusted (self signed certificate in chain), so I ran the checks with curl -k; the API itself answered normally. Retry without -k from your own environment.
The output is a human-readable text table inside JSON, not structured rows.

verification.notes: Exact example executed without a key, using curl -k because the sandbox did not trust the TLS chain.

hn.title: JPL Horizons on-line solar system data and ephemeris computation service
